strengths: The paper identifies a concrete weakness of Best-of-N self-improvement: different random samples often provide ambiguous fine-grained preference signals. Constructing pairs through swap, replace, and drop perturbations is intuitive and directly targets object omission and attribute-binding errors.

The framework is technically coherent overall: pairwise prompt densification helps preserve scene context, object-centric perturbations create controlled local differences, and SimPO provides a straightforward optimization objective.

The strongest empirical result is on T2I-CompBench++, where OSPO improves Janus-Pro-7B in every reported category; examples include color from 0.5215 to 0.8868, shape from 0.3272 to 0.6853, and Spatial-2D from 0.1654 to 0.3622. It also consistently outperforms the closely related SILMM baseline on this benchmark.

Evaluation covers three compositional benchmarks with different prompt characteristics. The improvement on DPG-Bench from 83.81 to 85.94 provides some evidence that the method transfers beyond the structured training-prompt distribution.

The component ablations support the importance of negative-prompt generation and densification, particularly for attribute and layout performance. The appendix supplies prompt templates, training hyperparameters, computational cost, dataset examples, and extensive qualitative comparisons, which improves clarity and partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: The proposed Preference Strength Score is mathematically under-specified and potentially unstable. It divides normalized local contrast by normalized global contrast, but no epsilon, clipping, positivity constraint, or fallback is given. A zero global gap makes the score undefined, while negative or near-zero gaps can reverse or arbitrarily amplify the ranking. The manuscript does not report how these cases are handled in practice. This is a material correctness and reproducibility issue in the central selection mechanism.

The headline claim of substantial improvement across all benchmarks is not supported uniformly. On GenEval, OSPO's reported total is 0.80, equal to the unmodified Janus-Pro baseline, while counting falls markedly from 0.59 to 0.40. DPG-Bench improves by only 2.13 points and relation slightly decreases. The main gains are concentrated in T2I-CompBench++ attributes and layout.

Evaluation is limited to one 7B backbone, one apparent training run, and no uncertainty estimates or repeated generation seeds. Because text-to-image sampling and training are stochastic, the absence of confidence intervals or variance estimates makes modest differences—such as several DPG-Bench and ablation changes—difficult to interpret.

The training prompts are deliberately constructed from the same four categories and similar template structure as T2I-CompBench++, which is also the benchmark showing the largest gains. Although DPG-Bench and GenEval provide some out-of-distribution evidence, their aggregate results are much weaker; consequently, the paper does not yet establish that the large improvements generalize beyond benchmark-shaped prompt distributions.

All quantitative evidence measures prompt compliance through automated benchmark evaluators, while no human evaluation, aesthetic score, diversity analysis, or general image-quality metric is reported. Preference training can improve evaluator-recognizable object bindings while degrading realism, diversity, or overall quality, and the selected qualitative examples cannot exclude this possibility.

The ablation evidence is not fully monotonic: removing negative-prompt generation improves layout and GenEval, and removing densification slightly improves GenEval. This suggests meaningful trade-offs that are not analyzed. Moreover, VQA selection contributes only marginally within OSPO, weakening the claimed importance and novelty of the local/global scoring component.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the extensive appendix: image-generation and evaluation sampling settings, random seeds, optimizer details, and the exact handling of invalid score denominators are not specified, and no code or generated preference dataset is provided in the manuscript.

Overall, the controlled-pair construction is promising and the T2I-CompBench++ gains are compelling, but the unstable central scoring definition, single-backbone/single-run evidence, benchmark-distribution alignment, and lack of image-quality validation place the work near the acceptance boundary rather than clearly above it.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant failure mode in text-to-image generation: omissions and incorrect object-attribute bindings in compositional prompts. Controlled perturbations (swap, replace, and drop) combined with pairwise prompt densification are intuitive ways to obtain more targeted synthetic negatives than unconstrained Best-of-N sampling. The paired densification intended to preserve scene context is a sensible practical detail.

The main T2I-CompBench++ results are substantial: OSPO improves all eight reported subcategories over both Janus-Pro-7B and SILMM, including color from 0.8304 to 0.8868 and spatial-2D from 0.2708 to 0.3622 relative to SILMM.

The evaluation includes three benchmarks, comparisons with the most relevant prior self-improvement baseline, component ablations, qualitative examples, training cost and hyperparameters, and extensive prompt templates. These are useful foundations for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The strongest improvements are on T2I-CompBench++, while the training prompts are explicitly constructed around that benchmark's four categories and closely matching templates. Evidence of broader generalization is much weaker: GenEval total is unchanged from the original Janus-Pro baseline at 0.80, and DPG-Bench improves only from 83.81 to 85.94. Several individual results regress, including GenEval counting (0.59 to 0.40) and DPG relation (92.72 to 92.15). This materially weakens the claim of robust out-of-distribution improvement.

The experimental evidence is not statistically reliable. Only one backbone, one training run, and point estimates are reported, with no repeated seeds, confidence intervals, or significance analysis. This is especially consequential for the modest DPG-Bench improvement and the effectively zero GenEval improvement.

The ablations do not consistently support the manuscript's broad component claims. Removing negative-prompt generation improves layout and GenEval; removing densification improves GenEval and nearly matches DPG-Bench; and removing VQA scoring changes several results only marginally. Thus the complete system is not uniformly preferable, and the claimed contribution of each component is category- and benchmark-dependent.

The preference-strength score in Eq. 2 divides normalized local-score differences by normalized global-score differences. The paper provides no epsilon, clipping rule, sign constraint, or handling for zero/near-zero denominators. Negative or very small global gaps can therefore reverse or destabilize selection. The gap distributions do not resolve this technical ambiguity, and the scoring ablation suggests the mechanism contributes little in OSPO itself.

The construction does not produce preferences between two outputs sampled under the same conditioning prompt: the losing image is generated from an intentionally altered prompt, and both prompts are separately densified with additional visual content. The manuscript does not clearly specify which prompt is used as x in SimPO or analyze whether densification introduces systematic nuisance differences. Consequently, it is unclear whether training learns the intended binding correction rather than broader artifacts distinguishing the two generation pipelines.

All central evidence relies on automated benchmark/VQA judgments, including the preliminary conclusion that Best-of-N pairs are semantically indistinguishable. There is no human validation of pair labels, perturbation correctness, densification fidelity, or evaluator agreement. The qualitative results appear selected and are not accompanied by a blinded or random-sample study, leaving evaluator bias and cherry-picking insufficiently controlled.

The novelty over SILMM is limited primarily to straightforward synthetic hard-negative construction and prompt densification. This may be useful engineering, but the paper does not provide a deeper learning analysis, demonstrate transfer across multiple unified MLLMs, or establish that the method outperforms simpler controlled-data alternatives. Reproducibility is further limited by missing exact generation/evaluation decoding settings, an unambiguous training-conditioning specification, released code/data, and checkpoints. Overall, the promising benchmark-specific result does not presently outweigh these validity and generalization concerns.

strengths: OSPO addresses a meaningful limitation of Best-of-N self-training: independently sampled images often provide weak or ambiguous object-level preference signals. Constructing targeted counterfactuals through swap, replace, and drop operations is intuitive, technically plausible, and reasonably original as a unified training framework.

The empirical results support usefulness on the studied Janus-Pro-7B setting. Relative to Janus-Pro + SILMM, OSPO improves all eight T2I-CompBench++ subcategories, raises DPG-Bench total from 85.14 to 85.94, and raises GenEval total from 0.76 to 0.80. The improvements over untuned Janus-Pro are especially large for color, shape, texture, spatial relations, and numeracy.

Evaluation covers three established compositional-generation benchmarks with substantially different prompt characteristics. The DPG-Bench improvement from 83.81 to 85.94 offers some evidence that the benefit is not confined to the short templates used for training.

The ablations meaningfully examine negative-prompt generation, pairwise densification, and VQA selection. They show that targeted negatives and densification drive most of the T2I-CompBench++ gains, while VQA selection is secondary once contrast is already strong. Extensive qualitative examples generally agree with the quantitative alignment results.

The method is clearly motivated and easy to follow. The appendix supplies the prompt templates, LoRA and SimPO hyperparameters, training duration, and numerous generated examples, providing a useful basis for reproduction.
weaknesses: The evidence is limited to one base model, one reported run, and no uncertainty estimates. This leaves unclear whether OSPO transfers across unified MLLM architectures or whether smaller category-level differences are statistically reliable. This is a material limitation on the breadth of the claims, although not sufficient by itself to outweigh the contribution.

The strongest gains occur on T2I-CompBench++, whose categories and prompt structures directly guide construction of the training set. Evidence for out-of-distribution robustness is mixed: DPG-Bench improves, but GenEval remains 0.80 after rounding relative to the untuned model, with counting dropping from 0.59 to 0.40. The manuscript consequently overstates improvement across all benchmarks.

The preference-strength formula is technically underspecified. It divides normalized local gaps by normalized global gaps, but global gaps can be zero or negative, and the maxima used for normalization can also be zero. No clipping, epsilon, sign handling, or rejection rule is given, so Equation 2 can be undefined or rank pairs contrary to its stated intent.

Images in a preference pair are generated independently from different dense prompts. Pairwise densification is intended to isolate the manipulated concept, but the paper provides no human annotation or quantitative intervention-validity study showing that other content, style, and quality factors remain controlled. Self-VQA evidence alone may miss such nuisance differences.

The evaluation focuses on automated prompt-alignment metrics and selected qualitative examples. A human preference study or an independent perceptual-quality/diversity assessment would be valuable because optimizing object-level correctness could degrade realism, aesthetics, or diversity without being reflected in the reported benchmarks.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the detailed appendix: no code or generated preference data release is identified, evaluation sampling details and random seeds are absent, and the role of Qwen2.5-VL is ambiguous. The preliminary-experiment footnote describes Qwen2.5-VL as the VQA model, while the framework emphasizes self-VQA and claims to require no external model; the exact model used to score training pairs should be stated unambiguously.

strengths: OSPO addresses a meaningful failure mode in unified autoregressive image generators: weak sensitivity to object-level attribute, binding, and spatial differences. Constructing paired text and image negatives, filtering them with decomposed VQA, and selecting uncertain pairs forms a coherent self-improvement pipeline.

The empirical evidence is broad and generally consistent. On Janus-Pro-7B, OSPO substantially improves all eight T2I-CompBench++ subcategories, raises DPGBench overall from 83.81 to 85.34, and raises GenEval from 0.80 to 0.82. Improvements also transfer to UniTok-MLLM-7B and Janus-1.3B, supporting applicability beyond one backbone.

The paper includes useful component analyses. Filtering plus uncertainty selection outperforms unfiltered sampling; prompt densification produces especially large Attribute and Layout gains; the loss ablations reveal a trade-off between VQA-oriented recall and detector-oriented precision; and a second self-improvement iteration provides modest additional gains.

The comparison between self-generated VQA rewards and Qwen2.5-VL is valuable: 0.87 average answer agreement and similar downstream results from the two filtered datasets provide some evidence that the method is not entirely driven by self-reward artifacts.

Implementation hyperparameters, prompt templates, dataset-size scaling, test-time selection results, and qualitative comparisons are provided, making the principal method reasonably understandable and partially reproducible.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is moderate. The optimization combines sequence-level SimPO, conditional likelihood preference, and SFT losses; it does not explicitly localize or optimize object regions. Much of the object-centric character comes from prompt perturbation and data curation, so the paper should distinguish this contribution more carefully from existing hard-negative construction and conditional preference learning.

Evaluation depends almost entirely on automated VQA, detector, and CLIP-derived metrics, with no human preference or object-level annotation study. This is consequential because the training pipeline itself uses decomposed VQA and synthetic compositional prompts, creating a risk of optimizing toward biases similar to those in the evaluation metrics. The reported self-versus-Qwen agreement does not establish correctness against ground truth.

Baseline comparability is insufficiently documented. The manuscript says that “several” methods were reproduced on the same backbone but does not identify exactly which table entries were reproduced, nor report their training and decoding configurations. Some competitors have missing categories, and no uncertainty estimates or repeated runs are given, making small differences such as 0.01–0.03 difficult to interpret.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the included hyperparameters: image-generation sampling settings, candidate counts at each stage, random seeds, exact retained dataset sizes after filtering, failure rates when candidate sets are empty, and full baseline settings are not reported. The description of producing “nine instances” per prompt and subsequently training on 19,000 triplets is also ambiguous.

The confirmation-bias analysis is limited. Agreement with another model is not accuracy, sample sizes for the agreement statistics are unclear, and both alternatives still use the training model for uncertainty-based selection. A human audit or benchmark with ground-truth atomic labels would more directly validate the generated preference pairs.

Several claims are broader than the evidence. OSPO does not uniformly outperform diffusion models—for example, its GenEval total of 0.82 is below some reported diffusion and self-improving baselines—and the second iteration is not consistently beneficial across subcategories. The manuscript should qualify claims of surpassing specialized diffusion models and steady iterative improvement.

The qualitative evidence is visibly selective and lacks randomized or failure-case presentation. There are also presentation issues, including grammatical errors, inconsistent naming such as “Jauns-Pro,” and explanations that occasionally infer mechanisms such as over-generation without directly measuring object precision and recall.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: fine-grained object and attribute alignment in autoregressive text-to-image MLLMs. The proposed pipeline—controlled prompt perturbation, paired image generation, decomposed-VQA filtering, uncertainty-based mining, and preference optimization—is coherent and practically motivated.

The reported benchmark improvements are substantial on T2I-CompBench++ and DPGBench. The evaluation also covers three benchmarks and three backbone configurations, providing more breadth than a single-model demonstration.

The manuscript includes useful component studies covering loss terms, filtering and selection, prompt densification, iterative training, data scale, test-time selection, and replacement of the self-reward model with Qwen-VL. Prompt templates and major training hyperparameters are documented.

The method requires no external reward model or collected training set in its principal configuration, which could make it useful for adapting unified multimodal models when external supervision is unavailable.
weaknesses: The evidence does not convincingly isolate the claimed object-centric preference contribution. In Table 4, removing both the conditional preference and SFT losses improves the T2I-CompBench++ Attribute score from 0.75 to 0.78 and DPGBench from 85.34 to 86.10; adding the conditional loss changes most results by only about 0.01. By contrast, prompt densification accounts for very large gains in Table 6. Missing SFT-only, densified-positive-only, random-negative, and matched-compute baselines leave open whether the main benefit comes from better synthetic positive images rather than OSPO's proposed preference mechanism.

There is serious reward/evaluation coupling. Training data are filtered using decomposed VQA, while T2I-CompBench++ Attribute and DPGBench also rely substantially on VQA-based evaluation. The largest reported improvements occur on these metrics, whereas the detector-based GenEval gain over Janus-Pro is only 0.02 and remains below DSR. The authors themselves report that the simpler SimPO-heavy variant over-generates objects and can thereby improve VQA scores. Without human evaluation, independent compositional evaluators, or precision/recall and hallucination analyses, metric optimization cannot be ruled out.

The confirmation-bias analysis is insufficient. Agreement with Qwen-VL is not ground-truth correctness, both models may share systematic biases, the reported mean scores show considerable calibration differences, and nearly identical downstream aggregate scores do not establish that the selected pairs are semantically valid. A human audit of positive/negative pairs and filtering errors is needed to support the central data-quality claim.

The comparisons are difficult to interpret as controlled evidence. Some entries appear to be published results while others are reproduced, several metrics are missing, and the paper does not report matched training-data sizes, sampling budgets, or compute for the reproduced self-improvement baselines. Consequently, the claim of outperforming prior self-improving approaches is not adequately supported as a fair comparison.

Statistical reliability is not reported: there are no multiple runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This is material for the small GenEval and secondary-backbone gains, and for ablation differences that are frequently only 0.01.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the supplied templates and optimizer settings. The manuscript omits seeds, important generation/decoding settings, precise candidate counts at each stage, filtering retention rates and final dataset composition, and a code/data release statement. The construction description is also ambiguous about how the nine candidates per initial prompt map to the eventual 19,000 training triplets.

The conceptual novelty is moderate: most components are established techniques—prompt perturbation, prompt densification, decomposed VQA scoring, uncertainty-based hard-negative mining, SimPO, and SFT—and the empirical evidence does not demonstrate that their specific combination yields robust object-fidelity improvements beyond evaluator-aligned synthetic training. Overall, the promising results and useful pipeline merit consideration, but the central causal and evaluation-validity concerns currently favor rejection.

strengths: OSPO addresses an important and well-motivated failure mode in unified multimodal models: fine-grained object presence, attributes, bindings, and relations in text-to-image generation. The combination of controlled prompt perturbations, paired prompt densification, VQA-based filtering, uncertainty-based hard-negative mining, and conditional preference optimization is coherent and practically useful.

The empirical results are strong and broad. On Janus-Pro-7B, OSPO substantially improves T2I-CompBench++ and reaches 85.34 on DPGBench and 0.82 on GenEval. The evaluation covers three complementary benchmarks rather than relying on a single compositionality metric.

Experiments on UniTok-MLLM-7B and Janus-1.3B provide useful evidence that the framework is not tied to one architecture or model scale. The gains on the smaller Janus model are particularly meaningful.

The paper includes informative ablations of loss terms, filtering and selection, prompt densification, data scale, iteration count, and test-time selection. Prompt densification has a notably large effect, while filtering/selection and the conditional loss show smaller but generally consistent benefits.

The confirmation-bias analysis is a valuable addition: self-generated VQA decisions show about 87% agreement with Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and replacing the self-filter with that external model produces nearly identical downstream results. Qualitative examples also support improved object inclusion and attribute binding.

The method is comparatively resource-efficient at optimization time, using LoRA on four A100 GPUs, and the appendix reports the principal optimizer and loss hyperparameters as well as the prompt templates.
weaknesses: The evidence lacks repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Several ablation and cross-backbone improvements are only 0.01-0.03, so it is unclear which smaller gains exceed sampling and training variance. This is a material limitation for claims of consistent superiority, although the main Janus-Pro improvements are large.

Some conclusions from the loss ablation are overstated. The full objective is best on GenEval, but removing SFT or using SimPO alone gives higher Attribute and DPGBench scores; thus the results demonstrate a benchmark-dependent trade-off rather than that combining all terms is uniformly best.

Reproducibility of the data pipeline remains incomplete. The manuscript does not clearly report generation and decoding settings, the number of candidates surviving each filtering stage, the exact final number and distribution of training triplets, or evaluation sampling seeds. Algorithm 1 also appears to select the losing text over all negative texts on line 16 rather than explicitly over the filtered set, creating an implementation ambiguity.

Evaluation is confined to automated compositional-alignment metrics, with no human assessment of prompt fidelity, perceptual quality, or artifacts. Because decomposed VQA is used both to curate training data and by parts of the benchmark ecosystem, evaluator-specific optimization cannot be fully excluded; GenEval and detector-based results mitigate but do not eliminate this concern.

The comparison protocol is not fully transparent about which baseline numbers were reproduced under identical sampling settings and which were taken from prior work. This matters because image count, decoding, and test-time candidate selection can materially affect text-to-image benchmark scores.

The novelty is primarily in the integration of established ingredients—prompt perturbation, densification, self-VQA filtering, hard-negative mining, SimPO, and conditional preference loss—rather than a fundamentally new learning principle. The integration is effective, but the paper should frame its originality accordingly. Some grammatical errors, notation inconsistencies, and overly broad claims about surpassing specialized diffusion models also need refinement.
